Background (from the session that started this one):
Path App is a Hack Western 13 project (deadline Sunday Nov 22, 2026, 9:00 a.m. Toronto time): organizers scan a venue with a LiDAR iPhone, upload it, and share a Public/Unlisted/Private link or QR; guests open a 3D view and follow a route to a destination, with Gemini-suggested landmark cues ("Turn left at the amber doorway") that an organizer approves. Team: Sam owns the API/storage (issue #3), Krishna and Anish own phone capture (issue #4), Anish runs the second-phone trial (#5), Arielle owns all frontend. Prize targets: MLH Best Use of Gemini, Organizers' Choice Most Adventurous, possibly MLH Entire. Judging: innovation, technical complexity, completeness, design; the website is shown on laptops at the booth but the product must be mobile-first for iPhone. Arielle already approved a design direction, captured in `apps/web/DESIGN.md` and the interactive playbook at https://claude.ai/artifact/Abt1dfRD8khy9gxW5pDNJV (open it with the Artifact tool's read action if useful): cream background, green primary, coral accent with strict contrast rules, 3D on dark night green, road-sign display type, a live point-cloud hero with footprints on the landing page, flip cards for the four creators, and a P0 list of guest view, upload/share/QR, Gemini cue review and landing hero. The team workflow uses Entire (installed and enabled in this worktree, checkpoints push to origin), one GitHub issue per task, and `scripts/tasks.py` for claims and checkpoints. A read-only scheduled task `path-team-watch` already reports team changes every 30 minutes, so don't set up another watcher.

Task:
I'm Arielle (GitHub AryBaum), working on https://github.com/darkprince558/path-app/issues/2 on branch `feature/guest-viewer` in this worktree. My writable scope is `apps/web/`. I already claimed the issue (label `task:active`).

Then tell me the acceptance check and any dependency another teammate owns, and propose the scaffold in a few lines before installing.

Task for this session:
1. Scaffold `apps/web/` with Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4 + React Router, using pnpm. Put the color and type tokens from `DESIGN.md` into the Tailwind theme / CSS variables (cream `#F3EBD0` background, forest `#2F4A3A` primary, coral `#F48057` accent only for fills/route, rust `#A8421F` for coral-looking text, night `#121C16` behind every 3D view; Overpass display, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next body, Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono data).
2. Build the guest route `/s/:shareId`: call `GET /api/shares/<shareId>` for `{shareId, format, assetPath}`, fetch the asset, and render the PLY as colored points with `＠react-three/fiber` + `＠react-three/drei` (PLYLoader, `Points` with vertex colors, touch-friendly orbit). Show loading, not-found/denied, and parse-failure states where they happen. Proxy `/api` to the local mock in Vite dev config.
3. Verify with the local mock: run `py -3 -B tools/scan_mock.py --port 8001` (on this Windows machine `make` fails with exit 127, so call Python directly), upload `fixtures/venue/scene.ply` as Unlisted with the curl command in `services/api/README.md`, then open the returned `/s/<shareId>` in a signed-out browser tab and confirm the green entrance, amber workshop doorway and purple booth doorway at the junction are recognizable and orbit works. Also check the phone width (375px) in the browser pane. Run `py -3 scripts/check_fixture.py fixtures/venue/manifest.json` and `py -3 -B tools/smoke_scan_mock.py` if anything outside `apps/web/` is touched.
4. Commit `apps/web/` including `apps/web/DESIGN.md` (currently uncommitted) on `feature/guest-viewer` with a clear message. Ask me before pushing or posting anything on GitHub. When I say go, push, then post a checkpoint with `py -3 scripts/tasks.py checkpoint 2 "<what we actually verified>" --head --next "<next step>"` (gh lives in `C:\Program Files\GitHub CLI`; add it to PATH in Bash).

Out of scope for this session: routing/destinations UI, Gemini cue review, upload UI, and the landing page — those come next, in the priority order in `DESIGN.md`. # Path web design direction

Owner: Arielle. This is the agreed visual and UX direction for the landing page and the app in `apps/web/`. The live, interactive version (hero prototype, flip cards, footprint trail, guest-view mockup) is the playbook artifact: https://claude.ai/artifact/Abt1dfRD8khy9gxW5pDNJV (private to Arielle until shared).

## Color

Cream is the page background, green is the main UI color, coral is the accent.

| Token | Hex | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `paper` | `#F3EBD0` | Page background (primary) |
| `surface` | `#FAF5E6` | Cards and sheets on top of paper |
| `forest` | `#2F4A3A` | Primary: text, headings, buttons, active states |
| `coral` | `#F48057` | Accent: route line, pins, highlights, CTA button fill |
| `rust` | `#A8421F` | Coral-colored text and links (coral itself fails as text) |
| `night` | `#121C16` | Background of every 3D view and dark landing bands |
| `sage` | `#A9C4AE` | Primary color in dark mode, contour lines |
| `ink` | `#15221B` | Text on coral buttons |
| `muted` | `#5E6B60` | Secondary text on paper (4.7:1) |

Contrast rules, measured with WCAG ratios:

- Forest on paper 8.1:1. Use for all body text.
- Coral on paper is 2.2:1 and white on coral is 2.6:1. Never use coral for text or put white text on coral.
- Coral buttons use ink text (6.3:1). Coral-flavored text uses rust (5.1:1).
- Point clouds wash out on cream. Render 3D on `night`. Coral on night is 6.7:1, which suits the route line and 3D labels.

## Type

- Display: **Overpass** 800–900 (based on Highway Gothic road-sign lettering).
- Body and UI: **Atkinson Hyperlegible Next** (Braille Institute, designed for low-vision readers).
- Data: **Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono** for coordinates, distances, share IDs.
- Avoid a soft serif. Cream + coral + serif reads as a generic generated landing page.

## Motifs and motion

- The landing hero is the product: the real scan assembles from scattered points, the coral route draws itself, footprints walk it to a destination pin. Use the fixture until a real scan exists.
- Footprints are the landing-page motif: one SVG path in the left gutter, prints revealed with scroll (GSAP ScrollTrigger + MotionPath). Under 40% opacity.
- Inside the app, routes are a coral line with flowing dashes and waypoint dots, not footprints, since some users roll rather than walk.
- One orchestrated animation per landing section. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` everywhere.
- Booth: a QR in the hero and Join section opens the guest link on the judge's phone. The hero replays after ~20 s idle.

## Landing page sections

Hero (live scan + QR + Log in / Sign up) → The problem (sticky scroll: 2D floor plan tilts into 3D, one measured stat) → Our product (Scan · Share with Public/Unlisted/Private · Navigate with landmark cues, real screenshots) → How to use (3 steps joined by footprints) → Creators (flip cards: hover on desktop, tap on iPhone, focus on keyboard; GitHub, LinkedIn, résumé, portfolio) → Join us (trail ends at a pin by the CTA and QR).

## App screens, by priority

- **P0:** guest view at `/s/:shareId` (full-bleed 3D on night, destinations in a bottom sheet, Gemini cue card with source frame and "approved by organizer", route by Dijkstra over the manifest graph) · upload with visibility toggle, copy link and QR · Gemini cue review (accept / edit / reject) · landing hero.
- **P1:** rest of the landing page · Explore (public scans + filter chips: Campus, Events, Hospitals, Trails, Step-free) · settings (step-free routing, text size, reduce motion) · one "elevator out" alert that reroutes.
- **Cut or fake:** custom login screens (use the provider's hosted login), comments and feed, events calendar, live indoor positioning.

## Stack

Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4 + React Router, built to static files.

| Job | Library |
| --- | --- |
| 3D viewer | `three`, `@react-three/fiber`, `@react-three/drei` (PLYLoader, CameraControls, Line, Html) |
| Scroll story, footprints | `gsap`, `@gsap/react` (ScrollTrigger, MotionPath, DrawSVG) |
| UI motion | `motion` |
| Landing smooth scroll | `lenis` (off in the app and under reduced motion) |
| Components | shadcn/ui (Radix) |
| Bottom sheet | `vaul` |
| Toasts, QR, icons | `sonner`, `qrcode.react`, `lucide-react` |
| Showpieces | Two or three restyled snippets from Magic UI, Aceternity UI or React Bits |

Mobile targets: the guest link opens signed out in under 3 s on an iPhone; cap device pixel ratio at 2 and downsample large PLYs. Hosting is proposed on Vultr behind Caddy, which must serve `index.html` for `/s/<shareId>` so direct links don't 404.
======
# Website

Arielle owns the organizer upload flow and guest 3D viewer. Build the website here. Start with an upload control, the three visibility choices, a copy-link action and a guest route at `/s/<shareId>`. Display upload, loading and processing failures where they occur.

For the first integration, upload the sample PLY as **Unlisted**, open the returned link in a signed-out session, and use the response’s `assetPath` to load the point cloud with vertex colors. A guest should be able to orbit the scene and recognize the corridor junction. Use the actual phone export to choose camera framing, point size and mobile performance targets.

The local API provides fixture bytes and exercises sharing rules. Replace its test page with the website’s guest route during integration. [Local API commands](../../services/api/README.md) · [Capture format and viewer notes](../../docs/scan-formats.md)

# Upload and sharing API

Sam owns the durable backend. The team can integrate against the local reference API now with Python 3.9+ and Make. From the repo root, run `make dev-api` in one terminal, then upload the fixture from another.

```sh
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -H 'X-Dev-User: organizer' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' \
  --data-binary @fixtures/venue/scene.ply \
  'http://127.0.0.1:8001/api/scans?format=ply&visibility=unlisted'
```

The response includes `shareId` and `sharePath`. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8001` followed by that path in another browser on the same computer. The development page links to the exact uploaded bytes. Arielle’s guest page will use the metadata and asset endpoints below to render the model.

| Request | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/scans?format=ply&visibility=unlisted` | Send raw bytes. Accepts `ply` or `glb`; visibility defaults to `private`. Returns 201 with `{shareId, sharePath}`. |
| `GET /api/scans/public` | Returns `{scans: [{shareId, sharePath}]}` for public discovery. |
| `GET /api/shares/<shareId>` | Returns `{shareId, format, assetPath}` to a permitted viewer. |
| `GET /api/shares/<shareId>/asset` | Returns the uploaded file after the same access check. |
| `PATCH /api/scans/<shareId>` | Owner sends JSON with `visibility` and the complete replacement list `viewerIds`. Returns the new sharing state. |

To grant private access, send `{"visibility":"private","viewerIds":["teammate"]}` as the organizer. Repeat with an empty list to revoke access. The smoke test covers both changes, the raw asset URL, and unauthenticated discovery.

The mock binds to loopback, uses `X-Dev-User` to simulate an account, checks file headers, limits uploads to 32 MiB, and discards data on exit. On the hosted API derive identity from a verified session, validate the uploaded model, persist grants, and enforce visibility on every read. Use the deployed site’s origin for portable share URLs. [Architecture and data model](../../docs/architecture.md)
=====
# Venue integration fixture

[Open the manifest](venue/manifest.json) to see the complete v1 example. The 93 colored points in [scene.ply](venue/scene.ply) depict a synthetic T-shaped corridor. From the green entrance, walk 4 m to the junction. Both destinations are 3 m from there. The workshop is on the left under an amber doorway and the info booth is on the right under a purple doorway.

## Manifest v1

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schemaVersion`, `eventId` | Integer `1` and a stable event identifier. |
| `scene.format`, `scene.path` | `ply` and a path relative to the manifest. Resolve the path against the manifest URL when loading it in a browser. |
| `waypoints[]` | Each waypoint has a unique `id` and a three-number `position` in meters. |
| `edges[]` | Each edge connects the waypoint IDs `from` and `to` in both directions. Its weight is the Euclidean distance between their positions. |
| `startWaypointId` | The waypoint associated with the demo entrance QR code. |
| `destinations[]` | Each destination has a unique `id`, a guest-facing `label`, and a `waypointId` reachable from the start. |

The graph and PLY vertices share a right-handed event frame. The demo entrance is the origin, +X is right, +Y is up and −Z is forward from the entrance. The capture exporter aligns the scan to the event frame before handing it to the viewer. Use a point renderer for the PLY. It contains XYZ positions and unsigned 8-bit RGB colors.

## Check a fixture

From the repo root, run either command with Python 3.

```sh
python3 scripts/check_fixture.py
python3 scripts/check_fixture.py path/to/another/manifest.json
```

The validator checks the manifest structure, finite waypoint coordinates, unique IDs, edge endpoints, and reachability from the marked start to every destination. It checks that the referenced scene file exists within the manifest directory. Open the scene in the viewer to check its colors, scale, and alignment.
=====
# Choosing a scan format

**Try a colored PLY from RTAB-Map first.** Its Canadian iOS listing identifies it as free, lists PLY export, and specifies a LiDAR sensor for 3D reconstruction. Krishna and Anish can export a real hallway before writing a capture app. Arielle can start with the synthetic PLY today. Choose the guest format after the team opens a real scan on a second phone. [RTAB-Map for iOS](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/rtab-map-3d-lidar-scanner/id1564774365) · [Venue fixture](../fixtures/README.md)

| Candidate | What to export | What the guest sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colored point cloud (`.ply`) | Export points with XYZ positions and red, green, and blue vertex properties. Record the encoding because the fixture uses ASCII and the phone may write binary. | A 3D view made of colored samples. With Three.js, load the geometry with `PLYLoader` and render `Points` with vertex colors enabled. [PLYLoader](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/PLYLoader.html) · [Points](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/Points.html) |
| Textured mesh (`.glb`) | Try a mesh export with geometry and textures embedded in one GLB. 3d Scanner App lists GLB export and in-app purchases. Check export availability on the device. | Solid surfaces can preserve the appearance of signs and doors between sample points. Load the scene with `GLTFLoader` and check that materials display on mobile. [3d Scanner App](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/3d-scanner-app/id1419913995) · [GLTFLoader](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/GLTFLoader.html) |

Polycam is another option for a LiDAR mesh. Its free iOS tier includes Space Mode and glTF export. Check the output package for embedded textures or companion files before trying a single-file upload. Polycam lists point cloud export under Business and Enterprise. [Space Mode](https://learn.poly.cam/hc/en-us/articles/REDACTED) · [Export options by plan](https://learn.poly.cam/hc/en-us/articles/REDACTED)

## First phone test

1. **Krishna and Anish** record a short corridor with a turn, a colored landmark, and two points a measured distance apart. Record phone model, capture app and mode, file format, size, and export time. For custom capture, Apple's ARKit sample shows how to locate points using scene depth and color them from the corresponding camera image. [Apple's depth-cloud sample](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/arkit/displaying-a-point-cloud-using-scene-depth)
2. **Sam** accepts the organizer's exported asset and returns the Path App share link. The first upload only needs the scan. When adding navigation, align the asset and waypoints to the same right-handed event frame in meters, with +Y up and −Z forward from the entrance. Check the measured distance and the direction of the turn. [Venue coordinate convention](../fixtures/README.md)
3. **Arielle** opens the link signed out on a second phone. Time from opening the link to an interactive view. Orbit the scan, identify the turn and landmark, then reload the link. Record browser, phone, network, load time, and whether the landmark was recognizable.

Use the PLY for the demo if it passes that walkthrough. If sparse points obscure the landmark or the scan is too slow to navigate, compare a cropped or downsampled PLY and a textured GLB of the same section. Record the chosen export preset and observed measurements in the capture PR.

# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working. Claude does not tell the person that they missed it or could not see it, because Claude cannot tell what they were watching.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, Claude usually cannot tell whether the person is reading this conversation in the desktop app, on the claude.ai website or on a phone, and the shortcut and the globe icon work only in the desktop app, so before those steps Claude says that if they are not in the Claude desktop app on the computer whose browser Claude is using, they need to open this conversation there first. Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, without guessing at what the person saw.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

It lives at `localhost:5173/upload`, and the coral **Share a scan** button on the home page takes you there. An organizer:

3. **Taps "Upload and get link".** A coral bar shows progress, and there's a Cancel button.
4. **Gets the link back** with:
   - a **Copy link** button,
   - a **QR code** someone can scan with a phone camera,
   - a **Preview** button that opens the guest view,

I built the signed-in home screen from your sketch, and "organizer" is now "owner" across the website and the team docs. It's saved on your branch but not on GitHub yet.

To see it, open `http://localhost:5173/maps` in the browser panel.

## The home screen

**On a laptop** it matches your sketch:
- A **green side menu** with My maps and Community, a coral **New map** button, and your name and initials at the bottom.
- **"Your maps"** shows a grid of map cards with filter buttons: All, Public, Unlisted, Private and Shared with me. I added "All" and "Unlisted" so every map fits under some filter.
- Each card shows a small dark preview with dots and a coral path, the map's name, who can open it, the type of place and the date.

**On a phone** the side menu wouldn't fit, so it becomes a **bar along the bottom**: My maps, a round coral **+** in the middle for a new map, and Community.

**Community** lists real public maps from the practice server. Tapping one opens its 3D map. I uploaded a map as Public through "New map" and saw it appear there.

- **"Your maps" shows sample cards**, as you chose. They have a small "sample" tag and a note saying your own uploads will show up once the server can list them.

- **The name in the corner says "Demo owner"**, because there's no real login yet. To see your own name, start the website with this line in a file called `apps/web/.env.local`: `VITE_DEV_NAME=Arielle T.`

## The "organizer" change

The person who uploads a map is now called the **owner** ("map owner") in the website, the README, the roadmap and the other docs, including Sam's API notes. Mentions of the real Hack Western organizers and the "Organizers' Choice" prize stay, since those are about the hackathon.

okay what's next?

Next I'd build **the route on the guest page**. It's what turns the 3D picture into directions, and it's the top item still left in your design plan.

What the guest would see:
1. **A list of places at the bottom of the screen** (a "bottom sheet" you can drag up), for example "Workshop" and "Info booth".
2. **A coral line through the 3D map** from the entrance to the place they tap, with dots at each turn.
3. **The distance**, like "7 m · 1 turn".

The app works out the shortest way along the paths marked in the map (using an algorithm called "Dijkstra"), so later it can also avoid stairs for people who roll.

**One thing to know:** the route needs a list of the map's places and walkable paths (the "manifest"). Sam's server doesn't send that yet. Our sample building already has one in the `fixtures` folder, so I'd use it for now and write down for Sam what his server needs to send later.

**After that, in order:**
1. **Gemini hint card:** a small card on the route saying "Turn left at the amber doorway", with the photo it came from and "approved by the map owner". This is your Gemini prize piece. It needs Sam's server to call Gemini, but I can build the card and the owner's approve, edit and reject screen against sample hints.
2. **Landing page hero:** the animated scan with footprints and the QR code for the booth. It's mostly for judges, so it's best done once the real features work.

The deadline is tomorrow at 9 a.m., so I'd keep each piece small enough to demo even if the next one isn't finished.

Meanwhile, ask the team to review PR #15 so it can be merged. I'd start the route on a new branch built on top of your current work, with its own GitHub issue. I'll ask you before creating the issue, same as last time. Should I start on the route?
uhh I feel like that's not my job right now. How about the accessibility stuff and other features of the software frontend UI/UX?

Fair enough. Since you own the website's look and feel, accessibility and UX polish fit your role well, and nothing here needs Sam's server. Here's what I'd suggest, most useful first.

**1. A Settings page (accessibility options).** This is already in your design plan:
- **Text size:** Default, Large or Extra large, applied to the whole site.
- **Reduce motion:** follow the phone's setting, or always on or off. It turns off animations for people who get dizzy or distracted.
- **Step-free routes:** "I use a wheelchair, stroller or can't take stairs". It's saved now so the route feature can use it later.
- Settings are remembered on that device.

**2. An accessibility check of every page we've built.** This means testing with tools and fixing what they find:
- **Keyboard and screen-reader users can use the 3D map.** Right now it only works by dragging or pinching. I'd add arrow keys to turn it, +/− to zoom, and a text description of what's in the scan.
- **A "Skip to main content" link** (a "skip link"), clear focus outlines everywhere, and buttons big enough to tap (at least 44px).
- **An automatic accessibility scan** with a standard tool ("axe"), plus a color-contrast check against your rules in `DESIGN.md`.

**3. Small UX touches:**
- Short pop-up messages ("toasts") such as "Link copied" or "Settings saved".
- Loading placeholders that look like cards ("skeletons") instead of plain "Loading…" text.
- A search box on Community.

**4. A menu on each map card:** copy link, change sharing, rename, delete. Rename and delete need Sam's server, so those two would only be buttons until he adds support.

I'd start with **1 and 2 together** as one task, something like "Accessibility settings and fixes". That's a strong story for the "design" judging criterion, and it's all yours to own. Should I start that? Like before, I'd make a new branch and ask you before creating the GitHub issue.

Okay let's do that. Also it's nice to have the step-free routes in the settings page but also how about if you are with a friend who is using a wheelchair, you dont personally need it but they do, so should their be a switch or something. and maybe sometimes you just don't want to use the stairs but elevator instead say you went to the gym and are tired?

Good point, and it's a common gap in navigation apps: the setting describes the trip, not the person. Plenty of people avoid stairs only sometimes, like when they're with a friend who uses a wheelchair, pushing a stroller, carrying luggage or tired after the gym. So I'll do both:

- **Settings:** "Avoid stairs by default" for people who always need it.
- **On the map:** an **"Avoid stairs"** switch for this trip only. It starts from your default, and flipping it doesn't change your saved setting. The wording is just "Avoid stairs", with no wheelchair label, so nobody has to explain why they're using it.

The route itself doesn't exist yet, so for now the switch only remembers your choice. Whoever builds the route reads it from there.

content.text:
The accessibility work is done, and the automatic accessibility scan (axe) now finds no problems on any page. It's saved on a new branch, `feature/accessibility-settings`, but not on GitHub yet.

## What's new

**A Settings page** (`localhost:5173/settings`). On a laptop it's in the side menu; on a phone, tap the ⚙ next to your initials. Settings are saved on the device, so guests without an account can use them too.
- **Text size:** Default, Large or Extra large. Every page grows, map pages included. At Extra large on a phone, map cards switch to one per row so nothing gets squished.
- **Motion:** Match my device, Reduce motion, or Allow motion. "Reduce" turns off animations and the little glide after you let go of the 3D map.
- **Avoid stairs:** your default for every trip.

**On the map, an "Avoid stairs" switch for this trip only**, as you suggested. It starts from your default, and flipping it doesn't change your saved setting. I checked that: with the default On, I turned the trip Off, and the default stayed On. It just says "Avoid stairs", with no reason given. There's also a ⚙ button in the map's top corner that goes to Settings and brings you back.

**Keyboard and screen-reader access (WCAG fixes):**
- **The 3D map works with a keyboard.** Tab to it, then the arrow keys turn it, + and − zoom, and R resets. A small hint with the keys appears when it's selected.
- **A "Skip to main content" link** is the first thing the Tab key reaches.
- **The order Tab moves through the map page** is now top bar → map → buttons. Before, it started on the map.

**Fixes the scan and contrast checks found:**
- Grey hint text on a selected option was a bit too faint (4.13:1 against the 4.5:1 minimum).
- Some headings skipped a level, and the home page had no main heading.
- **The coral focus ring was too faint on the cream background** (2.2:1 against a 3:1 minimum). It's now forest green on cream pages, cream on the green menu, and coral only on the dark map. That's a small change to your design rules, so you may want to note it in `DESIGN.md`.
- At Extra large text, the "Reset view" button was pushed off the edge of a phone screen.
